text: American Water Works Company, Inc. is the largest and most geographically diverse, publicly-traded water and wastewater utility company in the United States, based on operating revenues and population served. Originally incorporated in Delaware in 1936 as a holding company, the company employs approximately 7,000 professionals who provide drinking water, wastewater, and related services to over 15 million people across 46 states. Its operations are primarily conducted through regulated utilities, collectively referred to as the "Regulated Businesses," and also include market-based businesses that offer complementary services. These market-based businesses, individually not meeting the criteria for a reportable segment under generally accepted accounting principles in the United States ("GAAP"), are grouped together as the "Market-Based Businesses," consistent with how management evaluates their performance. The company's history dates back to 1886, and throughout this Form 10-K, unless otherwise specified, references to "we," "us," "our," the "Company," and "American Water" refer to American Water Works Company, Inc. and its subsidiaries, collectively.

American Water, a publicly-traded water and wastewater utility company founded in 1886 and originally incorporated in Delaware in 1936, is the largest and most geographically diverse in the United States by operating revenues and population served. The company employs approximately 7,000 professionals and provides drinking water, wastewater, and related services to over 15 million people across 46 states. Its primary business consists of regulated utilities operating in more than 1,700 communities across 16 states, serving 3.5 million active customers, with services subject to regulation by state public utility commissions (PUCs) and other regulatory bodies. The company also operates market-based businesses, which are not individually reportable under U.S. GAAP and are collectively referred to as “Market-Based Businesses.” The Regulated Businesses generated operating revenues of $3,255 million in 2020, $3,094 million in 2019, and $2,984 million in 2018, accounting for 86%, 86%, and 87% of total operating revenues, respectively. The geographic breakdown of operating revenues and customers for 2020 shows that the top seven states by revenue—New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Missouri, Illinois, California, Indiana, and West Virginia—accounted for 87.7% and 85.5% of total Regulated Businesses revenues and customers, respectively. The remaining operations, including utility activities in Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New York, Tennessee, and Virginia, are categorized as “Other.” The company’s customer base includes residential, commercial, fire service, industrial, public authority, and other utility customers, with residential customers making up a substantial portion. Most regulated water customers are metered, allowing for monthly billing based on usage, while wastewater customers are billed either at a flat rate or based on water consumption. The company’s Regulated Businesses served 3,244,000 water and 252,000 wastewater customers as of December 31, 2020, representing approximately 15 million people. Customer growth occurs through acquisitions, population growth in authorized areas, and sales to other utilities. The company plans to invest between $22 billion and $25 billion over the next decade for capital improvements, including pipe replacement and upgrades to aging treatment facilities, with a target pipe renewal cycle reduced from 250 years in 2009 to an expected 110-year cycle by 2025, enabling the replacement of nearly 2,200 miles of mains and collection pipes between 2021 and 2025. Capital investment in treatment plants, storage tanks, and other above-ground facilities is also expected to increase from 2021 to 2025. The company has completed resiliency projects, including a $15 million emergency power system at the Raritan Millstone Water Treatment Plant in New Jersey and $23 million and $27 million improvements in Muncie and Richmond, Indiana, to retire facilities in 100-year floodplains. Operations are regulated by PUCs, which oversee rates, capital expenditures, operating costs, and other financial and operational matters, with regulatory policies varying by state and subject to change. The company uses various regulatory practices to mitigate regulatory lag, including infrastructure replacement surcharges, future test years, hybrid test years, utility plant recovery mechanisms, expense mechanisms, revenue stability mechanisms, consolidated tariffs, and deferred accounting. These practices are used to improve cost recovery and service reliability. The company’s growth strategy includes acquiring water and wastewater systems in geographic proximity to its existing operations to leverage existing management and achieve operational efficiencies, with a focus on expanding wastewater services where water services already exist. The company intends to grow its regulated footprint by acquiring systems in current markets and, where appropriate, entering new domestic markets after evaluating business and regulatory conditions to ensure a viable return on investment and continued service quality. Increasing regulatory pressures, infrastructure needs, financial challenges, and industry legislation may prompt municipalities to sell their water and wastewater assets. On November 20, 2019, American Water and its New York subsidiary entered into a Stock Purchase Agreement with Liberty Utilities Co., which was assigned to Liberty Utilities (Eastern Water Holdings) Corp., under which Liberty will purchase all capital stock of the New York subsidiary for approximately $608 million in cash, subject to adjustment. The New York operations serve about 125,000 customers. Algonquin Power & Utilities Corp., Liberty’s parent company, provided an unconditional guarantee of the obligations under the agreement. The transaction is subject to various conditions, including regulatory approvals, with an initial termination date of June 30, 2021, extendable by either party, and a final termination date of December 31, 2021, unless extended. Liberty may terminate the agreement if a governmental authority initiates a condemnation or eminent domain proceeding against a majority of the subsidiary’s consolidated properties. In the fourth quarter of 2020, the Governor of New York proposed legislation that, among other things, required changes to the state’s water utility regulations.

The Company’s regulated New York operations serve approximately 125,000 customers in the state. Algonquin Power & Utilities Corp., Liberty’s ultimate parent company, provided an absolute and unconditional guarantee of Liberty’s performance under the Stock Purchase Agreement. The agreement is subject to various conditions, including obtaining regulatory approvals and satisfying or waiving other closing conditions. It has an initial termination date of June 30, 2021, and either party may extend it beyond that date; the Company intends to extend the agreement if all conditions to closing are met, except for obtaining regulatory approvals. In the fourth quarter of 2020, the Governor of New York proposed legislation requiring the New York State Department of Public Service (“NYSDPS”) to study whether private water suppliers should be placed under municipal control. On February 3, 2021, the Governor directed the NYSDPS Special Counsel to begin and lead a municipalization feasibility study to be completed by April 1, 2021. The Company’s New York subsidiary continues to work constructively with the NYSDPS and is taking necessary actions to complete the Stock Purchase. Subject to satisfying or waiving the closing conditions and assuming no prior termination by Liberty, the Company remains confident the Stock Purchase will be completed, though the closing date could be affected by the timing of the NYSDPS Special Counsel’s work. In 2017, New Jersey enacted the Water Quality Accountability Act (the “WQAA”), which sets operational standards for all water utilities in the state, including municipal and investor-owned utilities with more than 500 service connections, covering areas such as cybersecurity, asset management, water quality reporting, remediation of violation notices, and hydrant and valve maintenance. The WQAA requires the most senior water manager—either the executive director of a municipal utility authority or the mayor or chief executive officer of a municipally owned public water system—to certify that the system meets the requirements. To strengthen accountability, the New Jersey Senate held three hearings on the WQAA in 2020, and the New Jersey Assembly has heard legislation to strengthen the WQAA in one committee, with referral to the Assembly Appropriations Committee pending. The Company’s regulated subsidiaries in California, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Maryland, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Virginia have access to fair market value legislation for private sector investment in public sector water and wastewater systems. The Company supports full optionality for municipalities, including state legislation that enables the consolidation of the fragmented water and wastewater industries through third-party fair market valuations of purchased property. Fair market value assessment is an alternative to the traditional depreciated original cost method, allowing the Company to offer municipalities a purchase price reflective of the assets’ fair market value while providing the Company with increased opportunity to recover the purchase price over the life of the purchased assets, subject to PUC approval. In 2020, Indiana passed legislation creating an appraisal process to establish fair value for non-municipal utilities and establishing a presumption that a purchase price not exceeding the appraised value is reasonable. The legislation also requires that all new municipal water and wastewater systems be subject to the jurisdiction of the utility regulatory commission for ten years. Separate legislation authorizes recovery for above ground infrastructure without a full rate case for service enhancements completed for health, safety, or environmental concerns and removes relocations completed for road construction from distribution system improvement charge recovery caps. Consolidated tariffs use a unified rate structure for systems owned and operated by a single utility, which may or may not be physically interconnected, moderating the impact of periodic fluctuations in local costs and promoting more universal water infrastructure investment across a state. This structure makes it easier to incorporate new systems, supports economies of scale even for small systems, and prioritizes capital needs statewide. The Company believes consolidated tariffs deliver cost-effective, high-quality services to more customers. Twelve of the Company’s regulated jurisdictions currently have some form of consolidated tariff pricing, including California, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia. In 2020, West Virginia passed legislation allowing expanded asset valuation in connection with utility acquisitions, combined water and wastewater revenue requirements, and expanded municipal use of proceeds from the sale of water or wastewater systems. The legislation also allows inclusion of contributed property in asset valuation and rate base recognition for the full purchase price approved by the Public Service Commission of West Virginia. In December 2020, Congress passed and the President signed into law a $900 billion COVID-19 relief and $1.4 trillion U.S. government appropriations package for 2021, which included $638 million for a low-income water assistance program and $2.8 billion for capitalization grants under the Clean Water and Drinking Water State Revolving Funds. The Company is awaiting further guidance on the distribution of these funds. The Company’s Regulated Businesses generally do not face direct competition in their existing markets because they operate under franchises, charters, certificates of public convenience and necessity, or similar authorizations issued by state PUCs or other authorities, and because the high cost of constructing a new water and wastewater system creates a significant barrier to market entry. However, they face competition from governmental agencies, other investor-owned utilities, large industrial customers with the ability to provide their own water supply or treatment, and strategic buyers entering new markets or making strategic acquisitions. The Company’s largest investor-owned competitors, based on operating revenues and population served, include Essential Utilities, Inc. (formerly Aqua America, Inc.), Suez North America, American States Water Company, and California Water Service Group. The Company also faces competition from infrastructure funds, multi-utility companies, and others such as Algonquin Power and Utilities Corp., Eversource Energy, and Corix. All or portions of the Regulated Businesses’ utility assets could be acquired by state, municipal, or other government entities through eminent domain, rights of purchase granted or reserved when a CPCN was issued, or rights granted under state law. Acquisition consideration may be determined under eminent domain law or negotiated or fixed by appraisers as prescribed by state law or in the CPCN. The Regulated Businesses are periodically subject to condemnation proceedings. For example, a citizens group in Monterey, California successfully added “Measure J” to the November 2018 election ballot, asking voters to decide whether the Monterey Peninsula Water Management District (the “MPWMD”) should conduct a feasibility study on the potential purchase of the Monterey water service system assets (the “Monterey system assets”) of the Company’s California subsidiary, and if feasible, proceed with a purchase without an additional public vote. The service territory includes approximately 40,000 customers. In November 2018, Measure J was certified as passed. In August 2019, the MPWMD’s General Manager issued a report recommending that the MPWMD board (1) develop criteria to determine which water systems should be considered for acquisition; (2) examine the feasibility of acquiring the Monterey system assets and consider public ownership of smaller systems only if the MPWMD becomes the owner of a larger system; (3) evaluate whether the acquisition is in the public interest and sufficiently satisfies the “feasible” criterion under Measure J; (4) ensure significant potential for cost savings before agreeing to commence an acquisition; and (5) develop more fully alternate operating plans before deciding whether to consider a Resolution of Necessity. In November 2019, the MPWMD issued a preliminary valuation and cost of service analysis report finding that (1) the total value of the Monterey system assets plus adjustments would be approximately $513 million, (2) cost of service modeling indicates significant annual reductions in revenue requirements and projected monthly water bills, and (3) the acquisition would be economically feasible. On June 12, 2020, the MPWMD issued a draft environmental impact report for the potential acquisition of the Monterey system assets and a related district boundary adjustment. On September 15, 2020, the MPWMD gave notice of its intention to appraise the Monterey system assets and related property interests. On September 29, 2020, the Company’s California subsidiary declined to make the Monterey system assets and related property interests available for inspection or comply with any of the other requests in the MPWMD’s notice. On October 7, 2020, the MPWMD issued a final environmental impact report (“FEIR”), and on November 4, 2020, certified the FEIR, which purports to analyze the environmental impacts of (1) acquiring the Monterey system assets through eminent domain, if necessary, and (2) expanding its geographic boundaries to include all parts of the system. On November 25, 2020, the Company’s California subsidiary filed a petition challenging this certification in court. The MPWMD is required to file an application with the Local Agency Formation Commission of Monterey County (“LAFCO”) seeking approval to become a retail water provider and annex approximately 56 parcels of land into the MPWMD’s boundaries. LAFCO approval is a precondition to the MPWMD filing an eminent domain proceeding against the Company’s California subsidiary. If the MPWMD determines acquisition is feasible, it would need to file a multi-year eminent domain proceeding. In that proceeding, it would first need to establish its right to take the assets. If such right is established, the amount of just compensation to be paid to the California subsidiary would then need to be determined. Additionally, five municipalities in the Chicago, Illinois area (approximately 30,300 customers) formed a water agency and filed an eminent domain lawsuit against the Company’s Illinois subsidiary in January 2013, seeking to condemn the water pipeline serving those municipalities. Before filing, the water agency made an offer of $38 million for the pipeline. The parties have filed updated valuation reports with the court. Although the valuation trial date is not currently scheduled, it is not likely to commence until the second quarter of 2021. In certain jurisdictions, the law allows private property owners to file lawsuits against public utilities if the utility’s infrastructure is determined to be a substantial cause of damage to the property, without requiring proof of negligence. In California, such lawsuits have been filed in connection with large-scale natural events like wildfires, with some alleging that utility infrastructure triggered the events causing property damage. In some cases, the PUC has allowed certain costs or losses to be recovered from customers in rates, but in others such recovery has been disallowed. The utility may have obtained insurance to respond to some or all of such losses, though it remains at risk for losses not recoverable through rates or insurance or losses exceeding insurance limits. The Company’s Regulated Businesses generally own the physical assets used to store, pump, treat, and deliver water to customers and collect, treat, transport, and recycle wastewater. The Company does not typically own the water, which is held in public trust and is allocated through contracts, permits, allocation rights from federal or state or multi-state agencies, or through ownership of water rights under local law. The Company depends on defined sources of water supply and obtains water from surface sources such as reservoirs, lakes, rivers, and streams; groundwater sources such as wells and aquifers; and water purchased from third-party suppliers. The level of water treatment varies based on source quality and customer stipulations, with surface water generally requiring significant treatment and groundwater often requiring only chemical treatment. The Company’s ability to meet existing and future water demands depends on an adequate water supply. Drought, governmental restrictions, overuse, protection of threatened species or habitats, contamination, or other factors may limit the availability of ground and surface water. The Company employs various measures to secure adequate water supply in the short and long term. The geographic diversity of its service areas may mitigate some economic effects of weather extremes, as in any given summer, some areas may experience drier than average weather reducing available water, while others may experience wetter than average weather. The Company evaluates water quality, quantity, growth needs, alternate sources, and transmission and distribution capacity to provide service. Water supply is seasonal and weather conditions significantly affect supply. To ensure adequate supply, the Company uses long-term planning and maintains contingency plans to minimize the impact of climate variability and weather fluctuations. For most surface or groundwater sources, the Company uses models to determine safe yields under different rainfall and drought conditions. Surface and groundwater levels are routinely monitored to predict and mitigate supply capacity deficits through demand management and additional supply development. An example of long-term planning is the Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project (the “Water Supply Project”) in California, which includes construction of a desalination plant owned by the Company’s California subsidiary and wells supplying water to the desalination plant. The project also includes the California subsidiary’s purchase of water from a groundwater replenishment project (the “GWR Project”) between Monterey One Water and the MPWMD. The Water Supply Project is intended, among other things, to fulfill obligations to eliminate unauthorized diversions from the Carmel River as required under orders from the California State Water Resources Control Board (the “SWRCB”). Wastewater services involve collecting wastewater from customers’ premises through sewer lines, transporting it through a sewer network to a treatment facility, treating it to meet regulatory standards before returning it to the environment, and disposing of or recycling the solid waste by-product in accordance with applicable standards and regulations. Customer demand for water service is affected by weather and varies with temperature and rainfall. Demand is generally higher during warmer months due to increased outdoor water use, such as irrigation. As a result, the Company typically expects its operating revenues to peak in the third quarter of each year. Hotter and drier weather generally increases operating revenues, while cooler and wetter weather suppresses demand and can reduce water operating revenues. Three of the Company’s jurisdictions—California, Illinois, and New York—have adopted revenue stability mechanisms that allow the Company to collect state PUC-authorized revenue for a given period not tied to the volume of water sold, thereby reducing the impact of weather variability. Market-Based Businesses.

Wastewater is transported through a sewer network to a treatment facility, where it is treated to meet required regulatory standards before being returned to the environment. The solid waste by-product of this treatment is disposed of or recycled in accordance with applicable standards and regulations. Customer demand for the Company’s water service varies with temperature and rainfall, being higher during warmer months due to increased outdoor water use such as irrigation, leading to peak operating revenues in the third quarter of each year. Hotter and drier weather increases revenues, while cooler and wetter weather suppresses demand and reduces revenues. In California, Illinois, and New York, revenue stability mechanisms allow the Company to collect state PUC-authorized revenue not tied to water volume sold, reducing the impact of weather variability. The Company’s Market-Based Businesses provide home services to residential and smaller commercial customers and water and wastewater services to U.S. government military installations and municipalities, and are not regulated by state PUCs or subject to significant capital investment. Operating revenues for these businesses were $540 million in 2020, $539 million in 2019, and $476 million in 2018, accounting for 14%, 15%, and 14% of total operating revenues, respectively. Key segments include the Homeowner Services Group (HOS), which offers warranty protection and home services for water, sewer, gas, electric lines, heating and cooling systems, water heaters, and power surge protection, and operates through partnerships with municipalities, utilities, and organizations with terms typically ranging from three to five years and mutual optional renewals; as of December 31, 2020, HOS had approximately 3 million customer contracts in 43 states. The Military Services Group (MSG) operates on 17 military installations under 50-year contracts with the U.S. government, covering operation and maintenance of water and wastewater systems, asset replacement, and in some cases, system expansion. Asset replacement is completed either through discrete projects in the first five years or via a long-term recapitalization program over the contract life, traditionally funded from contract fees. New assets required for mission support are funded by the U.S. government through contract modifications. The Company has not used debt or equity to fund these capital projects, relying instead on limited working capital, though recent solicitations require bidders to finance discrete initial capital projects over five- or ten-year periods; three of MSG’s current contracts require such financing, which the Company is addressing through internal liquidity. Six of MSG’s contracts have price redeterminations every two years after commencement and every three years thereafter, while the remaining 11 are subject to annual price adjustments under “Economic Price Adjustment.” All 17 contracts can be terminated by the U.S. government for convenience or due to default or non-performance, with MSG entitled to recover allowable costs plus a profit margin. MSG’s backlog of revenue is approximately $6.2 billion with an average remaining contract term of 41 years. The Company faces competition in HOS from HomeServe USA and Cinch Home Services, and in MSG from American States Water Company, Suez North America, and Veolia Environnement S.A. The Company’s water and wastewater operations are subject to extensive federal, state, and local regulations related to environmental protection, health and safety, water quality, wastewater treatment, discharge, recycling, and disposal, including the Safe Drinking Water Act, the Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act, and the Clean Water Act, with state standards sometimes being more stringent than federal ones. For example, New Jersey established a standard for PFNA in 2018 and set maximum containment levels for PFOA and PFOS, implemented in January 2021. The Company maintains an environmental program focused on compliance and responsible resource use, with capital and operating costs expected to rise as standards become more stringent. The Company estimates $725 million in capital expenditures over the next five years, including $155 million in 2021, for environmental control facilities. The Company believes its operations are materially in compliance and often exceed minimum standards. Operations involve the use, storage, and disposal of hazardous substances such as chlorine, which generates waste requiring proper handling. The Company could incur remedial costs if contamination is discovered, as CERCLA and comparable state laws hold generators, transporters, and current or former owners or operators liable without fault. The Company is not aware of any material cleanup obligations, though future discoveries could result in additional costs. Facilities are also subject to U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Act requirements and inspections. The Safe Drinking Water Act sets national standards for drinking water quality, including over 90 regulated contaminants and water quality indicators, with a process to evaluate at least five additional compounds every five years. The EPA may require monitoring of unregulated contaminants under the Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule, which the Company participated in during the fourth round concluding in 2020. The EPA has established rules such as the Long-Term 2 Rule, Stage 2 Disinfectants and Disinfection Byproduct Rule, and Ground Water Rule to improve disinfection and reduce exposure to disinfection by-products. In 2016, the revised Total Coliform Rule introduced a “find and fix” process requiring corrective action when bacterial trigger levels are exceeded. The Company is within the EPA’s compliance timeframe for all these standards, including sample collection, data analysis, and treatment enhancements. Recent monitoring under the Long-Term 2 Rule indicates that approximately 30 of the Company’s surface water systems have completed or need to implement additional disinfection mechanisms against Cryptosporidium, primarily through ultraviolet light systems, with an estimated $150 million to $250 million still required for remaining facilities. The EPA is considering regulations for contaminants such as strontium, hexavalent chromium, fluoride, nitrosamines, pharmaceuticals, and volatile organic compounds, but the Company does not expect any such regulations to require implementation in 2021. In 2020, the Company conducted over ten million water quality and turbidity tests at its facilities, including continuous monitoring of turbidity, disinfectant residuals, and chemical treatment adjustments. The Company participates in the Partnership for Safe Water, with 68 of its 79 surface water treatment plants receiving the “Director” award, which recognizes comprehensive self-assessments, action plans, and high-quality water; the Company accounts for about one-third of all such awards nationally. Additionally, 66 plants received the “Five-Year Phase III” award, 61 received the “Ten-Year Phase III” award, 57 received the “Fifteen-Year Phase III” award, and 26 received the “Twenty-Year Phase III” award, recognizing sustained performance. Nine plants received the “Presidents” award for achieving rigorous filter effluent turbidity standards. The Company expects current and future compliance costs under the Safe Drinking Water Act and similar laws to be recoverable through the regulatory process and does not anticipate a material impact on operations or financial condition. Capital and operating costs are traditionally recognized by PUCs as appropriate for rate-setting. The Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), first published in 1991 and revised in 2000, 2004, and 2007, includes enhanced monitoring, reporting, and public education requirements. In 2011, the Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act restricted the use and introduction of lead pipes, plumbing fittings, solder, and flux. Despite these efforts, legacy lead plumbing remains in many communities. The EPA finalized revisions to the LCR on January 15, 2021, designed to better protect public health by reducing lead and copper exposure, with compliance mandated by January 2024. The Company is reviewing the revised rule and will develop an implementation strategy. Capital and operating costs for compliance cannot yet be determined, but such costs are traditionally recoverable through rate-setting. The Company currently estimates less than 5% of service lines in its regulated territories contain lead on either the Company or customer portion. The Company is replacing lead service lines (LSLs) as part of ongoing water main and service line renewal projects. The goal is to replace a significant majority of known LSLs in most service areas by the end of 2030, at a cost estimated between $600 million and $1.2 billion, which the Company believes is attainable where public policy supports it. For future acquisitions, the Company will set LSL removal goals during the acquisition process. Prioritization of LSL replacement depends on planned renewal projects, adjacent projects by municipalities or other utilities, LCR compliance monitoring results, and customer cooperation in replacing the customer-owned portion. In some cases, these factors may result in shorter or longer timeframes. The Company prefers to replace the entire external LSL if lead is found on either the Company or customer portion, as advised by industry organizations including the U.S. National Drinking Water Advisory Council, the Lead Service Line Replacement Collaborative, and the American Water Works Association, and this approach aligns with the Revised LCR. The Lead Service Line Replacement Collaborative is a diverse group of public health, water utility, environmental, and other stakeholders.

The Company believes it can achieve lead service line (LSL) removal goals ranging from $100 million to $1.2 billion in most of its service areas where public policy supports such objectives. For future acquisitions, the Company will collaborate with communities to establish appropriate LSL removal goals. The prioritization of LSL replacement depends on several factors, including planned water main and service line renewal projects, adjacent municipal or utility projects, LCR compliance monitoring results, and customer cooperation regarding replacement of the customer-owned portion of the LSL. In some cases, these factors may result in a shorter or longer time frame for replacement. The Company’s preferred approach is to replace the entire external LSL if lead is detected on either the Company’s or customer’s portion of the service line, as advised by several water industry organizations including the U.S. National Drinking Water Advisory Council, the Lead Service Line Replacement Collaborative, and the American Water Works Association, and this approach aligns with the Revised LCR. The Lead Service Line Replacement Collaborative is a diverse group of public health, water utility, environmental, labor, consumer, and housing organizations working together to encourage communities to accelerate full LSL replacement through local collaborative efforts. The Clean Water Act regulates discharges from drinking water and wastewater treatment facilities into lakes, rivers, streams, and groundwater. The Company’s operations require discharge permits under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit program established under the Clean Water Act, which must be renewed every five years. EPA and implementing states set maximum discharge limits for wastewater effluents and overflows under NPDES permits; discharges exceeding these limits can result in fines and penalties, and persistent non-compliance may lead to significant fines and compliance costs. The difficulty of obtaining and renewing NPDES permits may impose time and cost burdens on the Company’s operations. Discharge violations occasionally occur at Company facilities, some of which result in fines, but the Company does not expect such violations or fines to have a material impact on its results of operations or financial condition. The Company maintains an industry-leading research and development (R&D) program designed to enhance its services, support compliance, improve service quality and operational effectiveness, and provide environmental leadership. For over three decades, American Water’s R&D program has advanced the science of drinking water, wastewater, and desalination. Efforts focus on contaminants of emerging concern, including but not limited to COVID-19, PFAS, Legionella, cyanotoxin-forming algal blooms, pathogens such as Cryptosporidium, Giardia, enteric viruses, and various bacteria, microbial indicators, and disinfection by-products. R&D personnel are located at the corporate headquarters and at two laboratory testing facilities in New Jersey and Illinois, with the latter housing a quality control and testing laboratory that supports R&D activities. The Company collaborates with the EPA and state agencies to establish environmental, health and safety, and water quality standards and regulations, sharing research such as treatment and distribution system optimization and national water quality monitoring data. This engagement provides early insight into emerging regulatory issues, allowing the Company to anticipate and accommodate future compliance requirements. The Company also engages with the Centers for Disease Control, state environmental agencies, and national and international water research foundations. The Company believes continued R&D is critical for providing safe, reliable, and affordable services and maintaining its industry leadership, which provides a competitive advantage in business and operational growth. Contaminants of emerging concern include numerous chemicals such as pharmaceuticals, personal care products, pesticides, herbicides, endocrine disrupting compounds, and industrial chemicals, as well as naturally occurring microbes like bacteria, viruses, and parasites detected in drinking water supplies, for which public health risks are not fully understood or assessed. Technological advances have enabled detection of many of these contaminants at trace levels, prompting discussions among regulators and government agencies and influencing public perception of drinking water quality. The Chemicals Abstract Service Registry contains over 173 million registered chemicals and an estimated 1,400 species of disease-causing microbes that can affect humans. The Company continuously investigates new substances and contaminants using a team of scientists, engineers, and public health professionals to identify threats to its water supply, respond to emerging regulations and health advisories, and evaluate alternative or advanced treatment technologies. The Company uses water quality testing equipment and implements new technologies to detect potential contamination, including monitoring the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on environmental virus loads, characterizing factors contributing to carcinogenic disinfection by-product formation, using research findings to advise customers on limiting Legionella exposure in large buildings (where CDC statistics indicate rising water-associated disease), defining a framework for managing opportunistic pathogens, using ultrasonic technologies to detect and manage algal blooms to prevent taste and odor issues and cyanotoxins, monitoring taste and odor issues with expanded analytical methods and recommending treatment practices, implementing water source assessment tools including sensors and data analytics to evaluate chemical storage and identify source water contamination, developing methodology and measurement techniques for contaminants of emerging concern to study transport, occurrence, and treatment, and implementing activated carbon, biofiltration, and ion exchange mechanisms to control such contaminants. American Water Works Service Company, Inc. (“Service Company”) is a wholly owned subsidiary that provides support and operational services to the Company and its affiliates, primarily to Regulated Businesses under contracts approved by PUCs, and also to Market-Based Businesses as needed. Services include accounting and finance, administration, business development, communications, compliance, education and training, engineering, health and safety, human resources, information systems, internal audit, investor relations, legal and governance, operations, procurement, R&D, rates and regulatory support, security, risk management and insurance, treasury, and water quality. Service Company operates two national customer service centers in Alton, Illinois, and Pensacola, Florida, providing customer relations, field service, and operational support to Regulated Businesses. Services are provided at cost, enabling operating subsidiaries to fulfill responsibilities cost-effectively while accessing in-depth functional expertise. The Company’s security team provides oversight and policy guidance on physical, cyber, and information security, as well as business continuity, throughout its operations. It is responsible for designing, implementing, monitoring, and supporting effective physical and technical security controls for physical assets, business systems, and operational technologies. Periodic risk assessments evaluate the effectiveness of existing security controls and inform additional safeguards. Operational and technical security controls are deployed to prevent unauthorized access to information systems, with the aim of ensuring the continuity of automated business processes, maintaining data integrity, supporting regulatory and legislative compliance, and ensuring safe and reliable service to customers. The Company partners with U.S. federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies to coordinate and improve the security of its water delivery systems and safeguard its water supply and operations. The Company considers environmental, social responsibility, and governance (“ESG”) fundamental to its corporate strategy and values. Integration of these principles into daily operations reflects its belief that “how” a company operates is as important as “what” it does, derived from core values: safety, trust, environmental leadership, teamwork, and high performance. These values drive the company’s strategy centered on five themes: Safety—employee and customer safety is the top priority; Customers—customers are central to all strategic decisions; People—maintaining an open, transparent, diverse, and inclusive environment where employees feel valued and accountable is critical; Operational Excellence—finding better, more efficient ways to do business to provide safe, clean, and affordable water; and Growth—growth enables investment in stable jobs, training, benefits, infrastructure, and communities, benefiting all stakeholders including shareholders.
